language_wrapper: Consider the p×p lattice on the torus Z_p×Z_p, where p is an odd prime and arithmetic is taken modulo p on both coordinates. You wish to select as many lattice points as possible under the restriction that among the selected points, no four points can form an isosceles trapezoid whose base is parallel to either the x-axis or the y-axis; here rectangles are also regarded as isosceles trapezoids. What is the maximum number of lattice points that can be selected in terms of {p}?
hardness_rationale: This family strengthens the seed by moving from a finite rectangular integer grid to a toroidal p×p grid over the cyclic group Z_p×Z_p, and still forbids axis-parallel isosceles trapezoids. The analysis no longer relies on elementary interval bounds of pair sums; instead, it requires using the Erdős–Heilbronn inequality for restricted sumsets in Z_p, plus a double-budget argument over rows and columns to constrain disjointness of sumsets modulo p. The optimal value emerges from balancing these additive-combinatorial budgets, and the extremal construction uses modular arithmetic to realize disjoint restricted sumsets across lines. This transition to modular settings and additive number theory increases both conceptual and technical difficulty compared to the seed.
notes: Key insight: forbidding axis-parallel isosceles trapezoids is equivalent to requiring that for any two distinct rows (resp. columns), the restricted pair-sum sets of selected x (resp. y) coordinates are disjoint. Over Z_p, the size of each restricted sumset is bounded below by Erdős–Heilbronn, so the total budget across all rows (resp. columns) is at most p. Balancing these two budgets yields the extremal count (5p−3)/2 with a matching construction using carefully chosen 2-point and 3-point patterns per row whose restricted sumsets partition Z_p while ensuring column-side disjointness.
source_question: Among all the lattice points \((x, y)\) where \(1\leqslant x\leqslant9973\) and \(1\leqslant y\leqslant9973\), some lattice points are to be selected. The restrictive condition is that among the selected lattice points, no four points can form an isosceles trapezoid (a rectangle is also regarded as an isosceles trapezoid) with the base parallel to either the \(x\)-axis or the \(y\)-axis. So, what is the maximum number of lattice points that can be selected?
